title: ADR: SLO federation and weighted degradation policy
author: Priya Nair
body:
Overview

This ADR establishes a federated SLO model and a weighted degradation policy for the inference runtime and adjacent services. The goal is to provide clear, predictable behavior when capacity, cost, or external dependency issues require graceful reduction in delivered fidelity.

Motivation

- Historically, service-level objectives (SLOs) at Redwood have been defined per-service with hard failover rules. This produced brittle user experiences when multi-service requests (for example: routing, KV cache, model variant selection) disagreed on priorities.
- Customers require both predictable latency and predictable token-unit costs. A single hard-fail SLO does not express trade-offs between cost, latency, and output fidelity.
- We need an orchestrated, auditable way to reduce output fidelity with minimal user-facing downtime while honoring contractual SLAs (hosted vs dedicated vs private).

Decision

We adopt a federated SLO model plus a lightweight weighted-degradation policy:

1) SLO federation
- Each logical request path composes SLOs from participating services (edge-proxy, routing, runtime, KV-cache, model-store).
- Composition rule: compute a weighted SLO score where each service contributes a normalized metric (p99 latency, error-rate, cost-per-token) with a configured weight. The top-level SLO is the aggregation of these weighted scores.
- Ownership: each service owns its local SLI definitions and the weight it contributes to federation (default weights stored in /service-config/slo-weights).

2) Weighted degradation policy
- When the federated SLO breaches a configured threshold, the system triggers a graded degradation controller (GDC). The GDC reduces fidelity according to a ranked list of degradation steps with associated weights and cost/latency impact estimates.
- Degradation is incremental: steps are applied until aggregated federated score returns under threshold or until a minimum fidelity floor is reached.
- Degradation steps can be global (applied cluster-wide) or tenant-scoped depending on tariff and permissions.

Key concepts and terms

- Federated SLO score: numeric score in [0,100], lower is better. Produced by linear combination of normalized service SLIs.
- Degradation step: an atomic change such as "downgrade model variant", "disable non-critical tools/plugins", "reduce beam width", "serve cached prefix only", or "increase token quantization level". Each step has: id, owner, estimated latency delta, cost delta, fidelity impact label.
- Fidelity floor: service-specific minimum allowed state (e.g., text-only structured output, fallback to small model) below which requests are rejected.
- GDC: graded degradation controller service running in control plane that evaluates SLO federation and executes steps.

Config examples

Service slo-weights example (YAML):

service: runtime
weights:
  p99_latency: 0.5
  error_rate: 0.3
  cost_per_token: 0.2

Degradation registry entry (JSON string stored in config store):

{"id":"deg-03-downgrade-to-quantized-8bit","scope":"tenant|global","owner":"runtime-team","impact":{"latency_ms":-18,"cost_pct":-28,"fidelity":"low"},"prereq":[],"rollout_type":"ramped"}

Operational rules

- Thresholds: federated SLO score > 70 -> warn; > 85 -> trigger GDC warning policy (notify owners); > 95 -> activate aggressive degradation steps. Thresholds are configurable per environment and per customer tier.
- Ramp strategy: when applying steps, prefer tenant-scoped and low-impact changes first. If no improvement, escalate to broader/global steps.
- Audit and reversibility: every applied degradation is recorded in the change log with correlation id, actor (automated or human), and observed SLI deltas. Automated steps are reversible and must support staged rollbacks within 5 minutes.

Rollout and ownership

- Owners:
  - GDC service: eng-platform (primary)
  - Runtime degradation steps: eng-serving-runtime
  - Edge/Proxy steps: eng-infra
  - Config and weights: service owners (each service team)

- Rollout plan:
  1) Pilot: enable federation + dry-run GDC for two non-production clusters for 3 weeks (observe and tune weights).
  2) Canary: enable tenant-scoped degradation for 5 pilot customers (customer success coordinates opt-in).
  3) Global: enable automatic tenant-scoped policy for free-tier and hosted-tier with conservative thresholds; dedicated/enterprise customers default to manual approval unless contract permits.

- Communication: notify on-call via pager for WARN and higher. Post-incident report required when aggressive global degradation triggered.

Alternatives considered

1) Centralized global SLO only (rejected): loses per-service ownership and makes local optimization hard.
2) Per-tenant static rate-limiting without degradation (rejected): blunt instrument; either injures latency or leads to rejection spikes.

Impacts and consequences

- Positive: more resilient user experience under resource stress, clearer trade-offs between cost and fidelity, better audit trail for customer-visible regressions.
- Negative: increased system complexity, need for reliable telemetry and timely SLI ingestion, potential disagreement on weights between service teams.

Telemetry and observability requirements

- Mandatory SLIs per service: p50/p90/p99 latency, request error rate, token cost estimate.
- GDC must expose: current federated SLO score, active degradation steps (with severity), time-since-first-degradation, last-reversal-duration.
- Dashboards: federated-slo-over-time, degradation-step-hit-rate, tenant-impact-matrix.

Security and compliance notes

- Degradation operations must not remove audit traces or bypass PII scrubbing. Any step that affects data retention or movement requires security review and explicit marking in the registry.
- Private deployments: the GDC control plane exposes only decision artifacts; enforcement is local (customer runtime agent) and must run with customer-managed keys.

Future work and extensions

- Add ML-based policy optimizer that tunes service weights and prioritization using historical incident data.
- Integrate per-prompt quality evals so fidelity impact is measured by application metrics (e.g., hallucination rate, intent match).

- /architecture-and-standards/model-serving-standards/continuous-fallback-orchestration-for-multi-variant-serving-standards-2026

Appendix: Example GDC evaluation pseudo-workflow

1) Ingest latest SLIs from services (windowed 60s).
2) Normalize to service scores using configured SLI-to-score functions.
3) Compute federated SLO = sum(weight_i * score_i).
4) If federated SLO > threshold -> evaluate candidate degradation steps sorted by cost-effectiveness; simulate estimated federated SLO after applying step; pick minimal set that returns score below threshold while obeying fidelity floors.
5) Apply steps with ramping (10% tenant population -> 50% -> 100%) and observe SLIs for 2 minutes per ramp step.
6) If SLIs improve, mark step active; else rollback and mark as failed for 24h.

Document lifecycle and maintenance

- Review cadence: quarterly by eng-platform and eng-serving-runtime.
- Change process: weight or step changes require an ADR-level micro-approval from affected owners; urgent emergency changes can be applied by on-call with post-facto ADR amendment.
